You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this - finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool - does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only - your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

1	# LNAV -- The Logfile Navigator
2	
3	The Logfile Navigator is a log file viewer for the terminal. Given a
4	set of files/directories, **lnav** will:
5	
6	- decompress as needed;
7	- detect their format;
8	- merge the files by time into a single view;
9	- tail the files, follow renames, find new files in directories;
10	- build an index of errors and warnings;
11	- pretty-print JSON-lines.
12	
13	Then, in the **lnav** TUI, you can:
14	
15	- jump quickly to the previous/next error (press `e`/`E`);
16	- search using regular expressions (press `/`);
17	- highlight text with a regular expression (`:highlight` command);
18	- filter messages using regular expressions or SQLite expressions;
19	- pretty-print structured text (press `P`);
20	- view a histogram of messages over time (press `i`);
21	- analyze messages using SQLite (press `;`)
22	
23	## Screenshot
24	
25	The following screenshot shows a mix of syslog and web access log
26	files. Failed requests are shown in red. Identifiers, like IP
27	address and PIDs are semantically highlighted.
28	
29	[![Screenshot](https://lnav.org/assets/images/lnav-front-page.png)](https://lnav.org/assets/images/lnav-front-page.png)
30	
31	## Why not **just** use `tail`/`grep`/`less`?
32	
33	The standard Unix utilities are great for processing raw text lines,
34	however, they do not understand log messages. Tail can watch
35	multiple files at a time, but it won't display messages in order by
36	time and you can't scroll backwards. Grep will only find matching
37	lines, but won't return a full multi-line log message. Less can only
38	display a single file at a time. Also, none of these basic tools
39	handle compressed files.
40	
41	## Try online before installing
42	
43	You can SSH into a demo node to play with lnav before installing.
44	
45	The "playground" account starts lnav with a couple of log files as
46	an example:
47	
48	`$ ssh playground@demo.lnav.org`
49	
50	The "tutorial 1" account is an interactive tutorial that can teach
51	you the basics of operation:
52	
53	`$ ssh tutorial1@demo.lnav.org`
54	
55	## Installation
56	
57	Download a statically-linked binary for Linux/MacOS/Windows from the release page:
58	https://github.com/tstack/lnav/releases/latest
59	
60	### Brew on MacOS
61	
62	```console
63	$ brew install lnav
64	```
65	
66	## Usage
67	
68	Simply point **lnav** at the files or directories you want to
69	monitor, it will figure out the rest:
70	
71	```console
72	$ lnav /path/to/file1 /path/to/dir ...
73	```
74	
75	The **lnav** TUI will pop up right away and begin indexing the
76	files. Progress is displayed in the "Files" panel at the
77	bottom. Once the indexing has finished, the LOG view will display
78	the log messages that were recognized. You can then use the
79	usual hotkeys to move around the view (arrow keys or
80	`j`/`k`/`h`/`l` to move down/up/left/right).
81	
82	Files that do not contain log messages can be seen in the
83	TEXT view (reachable by pressing `t`).
84	
85	### Usage with `systemd-journald`
86	
87	On systems running `systemd-journald`, you can use `lnav` as the pager:
88	
89	```
90	$ journalctl | lnav
91	```
92	
93	or in follow mode:
94	
95	```
96	$ journalctl -f | lnav
97	```
98	
99	Since `journalctl`'s default output format omits the year, if you are
100	viewing logs which span multiple years you will need to change the
101	output format to include the year, otherwise `lnav` gets confused:
102	
103	```
104	$ journalctl -o short-iso | lnav
105	```
106	
107	It is also possible to use `journalctl`'s json output format and `lnav`
108	will make use of additional fields such as PRIORITY and \_SYSTEMD_UNIT:
109	
110	```
111	$ journalctl -o json | lnav
112	```
113	
114	In case some MESSAGE fields contain special characters such as
115	ANSI color codes which are considered as unprintable by journalctl,
116	specifying `journalctl`'s `-a` option might be preferable in order
117	to output those messages still in a non-binary representation:
118	
119	```
120	$ journalctl -a -o json | lnav
121	```
122	
123	If using systemd v236 or newer, the output fields can be limited to
124	the ones actually recognized by `lnav` for increased efficiency:
125	
126	```
127	$ journalctl -o json --output-fields=MESSAGE,PRIORITY,_PID,SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER,_SYSTEMD_UNIT | lnav
128	```
129	
130	If your system has been running for a long time, for increased
131	efficiency you may want to limit the number of log lines fed into
132	`lnav`, e.g. via `journalctl`'s `-n` or `--since=...` options.
133	
134	In case of a persistent journal, you may want to limit the number
135	of log lines fed into `lnav` via `journalctl`'s `-b` option.
136	
137	## Support
138	
139	Please file issues on this repository or use the discussions section.
140	The following alternatives are also available:
141	
142	- support@lnav.org
143	- Discord: https://discord.gg/erBPnKwz7R
144	- Google Groups: https://groups.google.com/g/lnav
145	
146	## Links
147	
148	- Main Site: https://lnav.org
149	- Documentation: https://docs.lnav.org

lnav 0.14.0

A fancy log file viewer for the terminal.

Overview

The Logfile Navigator, lnav, is an enhanced log file viewer that takes
advantage of any semantic information that can be gleaned from the
files being viewed, such as timestamps and log levels. Using this
extra semantic information, lnav can do things like interleaving
messages from different files, generate histograms of messages over
time, and providing hotkeys for navigating through the file. It is
hoped that these features will allow the user to quickly and
efficiently zero in on problems.

Opening Paths/URLs

The main arguments to lnav are the local/remote files, directories,
glob patterns, or URLs to be viewed. If no arguments are given, the
default syslog file for your system will be opened. These arguments
will be polled periodically so that any new data or files will be
automatically loaded. If a previously loaded file is removed or
replaced, it will be closed and the replacement opened.

Note: When opening SFTP URLs, if the password is not provided for the
host, the SSH agent can be used to do authentication.

Options

Lnav takes a list of files to view and/or you can use the flag
arguments to load well-known log files, such as the syslog log files.
The flag arguments are:

 •  -r  Recursively load files from the given directory
   hierarchies.
 •  -R  Load older rotated log files as well.

When using the flag arguments, lnav will look for the files relative
to the current directory and its parent directories. In other words,
if you are working within a directory that has the well-known log
files, those will be preferred over any others.

If you do not want the default syslog file to be loaded when no files
are specified, you can pass the  -N  flag.

Any files given on the command-line are scanned to determine their log
file format and to create an index for each line in the file. You do
not have to manually specify the log file format. The currently
supported formats are: syslog, apache, strace, tcsh history, and
generic log files with timestamps.

Lnav will also display data piped in on the standard input.

To automatically execute queries or lnav commands after the files have
been loaded, you can use the following options:

 •  -c cmd  A command, query, or file to execute. The
   first character determines the type of operation: a colon
   ( : ) is used for the built-in commands; a semi-colon (
    ; ) for SQL/PRQL queries; and a pipe symbol ( | ) for
   executing a file containing other commands. For example,
   to open the file "foo.log" and go to the tenth line in
   the file, you can do:
   
    ▌lnav -c ':goto 10' foo.log              
   
   This option can be given multiple times to execute
   multiple operations in sequence.
 •  -f file  A file that contains commands, queries, or
   files to execute. This option is a shortcut for
    -c '|file' . You can use a dash ( - ) to execute
   commands from the standard input.

To execute commands/queries without opening the interactive text UI,
you can pass the  -n  option. This combination of options allows you
to write scripts for processing logs with lnav. For example, to get a
list of IP addresses that dhclient has bound to in CSV format:

 ▌#! /usr/bin/lnav -nf

usage: /workspace/executable [options] [logfile1 logfile2 ...]

A log file viewer for the terminal that indexes log messages to
make it easier to navigate through files quickly.

Key Bindings
  ?    View/leave the online help text.
  q    Quit the program.

Options
  -h         Print this message, then exit.
  -H         Display the internal help text.

  -I dir     An additional configuration directory.
  -W         Print warnings related to lnav's configuration.
  -u         Update formats installed from git repositories.
  -d file    Write debug messages to the given file.
  -V         Print version information.

  -S,--since Only index log content since this time.
  -U,--until Only index log content until this time.
  -r         Recursively load files from the given directory hierarchies.
  -R         Load older rotated log files as well.
  -c cmd     Execute a command after the files have been loaded.
  -f file    Execute the commands in the given file.
  -e cmd     Execute a shell command-line.
  -t         Treat data piped into standard in as a log file.
  -n         Run without the curses UI. (headless mode)
  -N         Do not open the default syslog file if no files are given.
  -q         Do not print informational messages.

Optional arguments
  logfileN   The log files, directories, or remote paths to view.
             If a directory is given, all of the files in the
             directory will be loaded.

Management-Mode Options
  -i         Install the given format files and exit.  Pass 'extra'
             to install the default set of third-party formats.
  -m         Switch to the management command-line mode.  This mode
             is used to work with lnav's configuration.

Examples
 • To load and follow the syslog file:
     $ lnav                                  

 • To load all of the files in /var/log:
     $ lnav /var/log                         

 • To watch the output of make:

payload.output:
usage: /workspace/executable [options] [logfile1 logfile2 ...]

A log file viewer for the terminal that indexes log messages to
make it easier to navigate through files quickly.

Key Bindings
  ?    View/leave the online help text.
  q    Quit the program.

Options
  -h         Print this message, then exit.
  -H         Display the internal help text.

  -I dir     An additional configuration directory.
  -W         Print warnings related to lnav's configuration.
  -u         Update formats installed from git repositories.
  -d file    Write debug messages to the given file.
  -V         Print version information.

  -S,--since Only index log content since this time.
  -U,--until Only index log content until this time.
  -r         Recursively load files from the given directory hierarchies.
  -R         Load older rotated log files as well.
  -c cmd     Execute a command after the files have been loaded.
  -f file    Execute the commands in the given file.
  -e cmd     Execute a shell command-line.
  -t         Treat data piped into standard in as a log file.
  -n         Run without the curses UI. (headless mode)
  -N         Do not open the default syslog file if no files are given.
  -q         Do not print informational messages.

Optional arguments
  logfileN   The log files, directories, or remote paths to view.
             If a directory is given, all of the files in the
             directory will be loaded.

Management-Mode Options
  -i         Install the given format files and exit.  Pass 'extra'
             to install the default set of third-party formats.
  -m         Switch to the management command-line mode.  This mode
             is used to work with lnav's configuration.

Examples
 • To load and follow the syslog file:
     $ lnav                                  

 • To load all of the files in /var/log:
     $ lnav /var/log                         

 • To watch the output of make:
     $ lnav -e 'make -j4'                    

Paths
 • This binary:
    🧭 /workspace/executable
 • Format files are read from:
    📂 /etc/lnav
    📂 /usr/etc/lnav
 • Configuration, session, and format files are stored in:
    📂 /opt/uiuc-agent/home/.lnav

 • Local copies of remote files, files extracted from
   archives, execution output, and so on are stored in:
    📂 /tmp/lnav-user-0-work

Documentation: https://docs.lnav.org
Contact
  💬 https://github.com/tstack/lnav/discussions
  📫 lnav@googlegroups.com

mouse to mark lines of text and move the view by grabbing the
scrollbar.

NOTE: You need to manually enable this feature by setting the LNAV_EXP
environment variable to "mouse".  F2  toggles mouse support.

Log Analysis

Lnav has support for performing SQL queries on log files using the
SQLite3 "virtual" table feature. For all supported log file types,
lnav will create tables that can be queried using the subset of SQL
that is supported by SQLite3. For example, to get the top ten URLs
being accessed in any loaded Apache log files, you can execute:

 ▌;SELECT cs_uri_stem, count(*) AS total FROM access_log    
 ▌   GROUP BY cs_uri_stem ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 10;     

The query result view shows the results and graphs any numeric values
found in the result, much like the histogram view.

The builtin set of log tables are listed below. Note that only the log
messages that match a particular format can be queried by a particular
table. You can find the file format and table name for the top log
message by looking in the upper right hand corner of the log file
view.

Some commonly used format tables are:

 Name         Description                                       
════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
 access_log   Apache common access log format                   
 syslog_log   Syslog format                                     
 strace_log   Strace log format                                 
 generic_log  'Generic' log format. This table contains messages
              from files that have a very simple format with a  
              leading timestamp followed by the message.        

NOTE: You can get a dump of the schema for the internal tables, and
any attached databases, by running the  .schema  SQL command.

The columns available for the top log line in the view will
automatically be displayed after pressing the semicolon ( ; ) key. All
log tables contain at least the following columns:

 Column          Description                                       
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
 log_line        The line number in the file, starting at zero.    
 log_part        The name of the partition.  You can change this   
                 column using an UPDATE SQL statement or with the  
                 'partition-name' command.  After a value is set,  
                 the following log messages will have the same     
                 partition name up until another name is set.      
 log_time        The time of the log entry.                        
 log_idle_msecs  The amount of time, in milliseconds, between the  
                 current log message and the previous one.         
 log_level       The log level (e.g. info, error, etc...).         
 log_mark        The bookmark status for the line.  This column can
                 be written to using an UPDATE query.              
 log_path        The full path to the file.                        
 log_text        The raw line of text.  Note that this column is   
                 not included in the result of a 'select *', but it
                 does exist.                                       

The following tables include the basic columns as listed above and
include a few more columns since the log file format is more
structured.

 •  syslog_log 
   
    Column        Description                                       
   ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    log_hostname  The hostname the message was received from.       
    log_procname  The name of the process that sent the message.    
    log_pid       The process ID of the process that sent the       
                  message.                                          
 •  access_log  (The column names are the same as those
   in the Microsoft LogParser tool.)
   
    Column         Description                               
   ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
    c_ip           The client IP address.                    
    cs_username    The client user name.                     
    cs_method      The HTTP method.                          
    cs_uri_stem    The stem portion of the URI.              
    cs_uri_query   The query portion of the URI.             
    cs_version     The HTTP version string.                  
    sc_status      The status number returned to the client. 
    sc_bytes       The number of bytes sent to the client.   
    cs_referrer    The URL of the referring page.            
    cs_user_agent  The user agent string.                    
 •  strace_log  (Currently, you need to run strace with

▌[1] - https://prql-lang.org/book/reference/stdlib/transforms/index.html 

Using the top ten URLs query from earlier as an example, the PRQL
version would be as follows:

 ▌;from access_log | stats.count_by cs_uri_stem | take 10    

The first stage selects the data source, the web  access_log  table in
this case.  The  stats.count_by  transform is a convenience provided
by lnav that groups by the given column, counts the rows in each
group, and sorts by count in descending order.  The  take 10 turns
into the  LIMIT 10 .

Dynamic logline Table (experimental)

(NOTE: This feature is still very new and not completely reliable yet,
use with care.)

For log formats that lack message structure, lnav can parse the log
message and attempt to extract any data fields that it finds. This
feature is available through the  logline  log table. This table is
dynamically created and defined based on the message at the top of the
log view. For example, given the following log message from "sudo",
lnav will create the "logline" table with columns for "TTY", "PWD",
"USER", and "COMMAND":

 ▌May 24 06:48:38 Tim-Stacks-iMac.local sudo[76387]: stack : TTY=ttys003 ; PWD=/Users/stack/github/lbuild ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/bin/echo Hello, World!    

Queries executed against this table will then only return results for
other log messages that have the same format. So, if you were to
execute the following query while viewing the above line, you might
get the following results:

 ▌;SELECT USER,COMMAND FROM logline;      

 USER  COMMAND                   
═════════════════════════════════
 root  /bin/echo Hello, World!   
 mal   /bin/echo Goodbye, World! 

The log parser works by examining each message for key/value pairs
separated by an equal sign (=) or a colon (:). For example, in the
previous example of a "sudo" message, the parser sees the "USER=root"
string as a pair where the key is "USER" and the value is "root". If
no pairs can be found, then anything that looks like a value is
extracted and assigned a numbered column. For example, the following
line is from "dhcpd":

 ▌Sep 16 22:35:57 drill dhcpd: DHCPDISCOVER from 00:16:ce:54:4e:f3 via hme3    

In this case, the lnav parser recognizes that "DHCPDISCOVER", the MAC
address and the "hme3" device name are values and not normal words.
So, it builds a table with three columns for each of these values. The
regular words in the message, like "from" and "via", are then used to
find other messages with a similar format.

If you would like to execute queries against log messages of different
formats at the same time, you can use the 'create-logline-table'
command to permanently create a table using the top line of the log
view as a template.

Other SQL Features

Environment variables can be used in SQL statements by prefixing the
variable name with a dollar-sign ($). For example, to read the value
of the  HOME  variable, you can do:

 ▌;SELECT $HOME;                          

To select the syslog messages that have a hostname field that is equal
to the  HOSTNAME  variable:

 ▌;SELECT * FROM syslog_log WHERE log_hostname = $HOSTNAME;    

NOTE: Variable substitution is done for fields in the query and is not
a plain text substitution. For example, the following statement WILL
NOT WORK:

 ▌;SELECT * FROM $TABLE_NAME; -- Syntax error    

Access to lnav's environment variables is also available via the
"environ" table. The table has two columns (name, value) and can be
read and written to using SQL SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE
statements. For example, to set the "FOO" variable to the value "BAR":

 ▌;INSERT INTO environ SELECT 'FOO', 'BAR';    

As a more complex example, you can set the variable "LAST" to the last
syslog line number by doing:

 ▌;INSERT INTO environ SELECT 'LAST', (SELECT max(log_line) FROM syslog_log);    

A delete will unset the environment variable:

 ▌;DELETE FROM environ WHERE name='LAST';    

The table allows you to easily use the results of a SQL query in lnav
commands, which is especially useful when scripting lnav.

CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE regexp_capture USING regexp_capture_impl();
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE regexp_capture_into_json USING regexp_capture_into_json_impl();
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE xpath USING xpath_impl();
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE fstat USING fstat_impl();
CREATE TABLE lnav_events (
   ts TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT(strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%f', 'now')),
   content TEXT
);
CREATE TABLE http_status_codes
(
    status  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    message TEXT
);
CREATE TABLE lnav_example_log
(
    log_line        INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    log_part        TEXT COLLATE naturalnocase,
    log_time        DATETIME,
    log_actual_time DATETIME hidden,
    log_idle_msecs  int,
    log_level       TEXT collate loglevel,
    log_mark        boolean,
    log_comment     TEXT,
    log_tags        TEXT,
    log_filters     TEXT,

    ex_procname     TEXT collate 'BINARY',
    ex_duration     INTEGER,

    log_time_msecs  int hidden,
    log_path        TEXT hidden collate naturalnocase,
    log_text        TEXT hidden,
    log_body        TEXT hidden
);
CREATE VIEW lnav_top_view AS
SELECT *
FROM lnav_views
WHERE name = (SELECT name FROM lnav_view_stack ORDER BY rowid DESC LIMIT 1);
CREATE VIEW lnav_focused_msg AS
SELECT *,
       log_msg_schema,
       log_part,
       log_actual_time,
       log_idle_msecs,
       log_mark,
       log_comment,
       log_tags,
       log_annotations,
       log_filters,
       log_opid,
       log_user_opid,
       log_opid_definition,
       log_format,
       log_format_regex,
       log_time_msecs,
       log_path,
       log_unique_path,
       log_text,
       log_body,
       log_raw_text,
       log_line_hash,
       log_line_link,
       log_src_file,
       log_src_line,
       log_thread_id
FROM all_logs
WHERE log_line = log_msg_line();
CREATE VIEW lnav_file_demux_metadata AS
SELECT filepath, jget(content, '/demux_meta') AS metadata
FROM lnav_file_metadata
WHERE descriptor = 'org.lnav.piper.header';
CREATE TABLE lnav_user_notifications
(
    -- A unique identifier for the notification.
    id         TEXT     NOT NULL DEFAULT 'org.lnav.user' PRIMARY KEY,
    -- The priority of this message relative to others, the highest priority
    -- message will be shown in the top-right corner.
    priority   INTEGER  NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    -- The time when this notification was created.
    created    DATETIME NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    -- The time when this notification is no longer applicable.

args.command:
cd /tmp/t/sql && python3 - <<'EOF'
import json
res = json.load(open('example_results.json'))
mismatch = []
errors = []
for r in res:
    exp = [e.rstrip() for e in r['expected']]
    act_lines = [l.rstrip() for l in r['stdout'].split('\n') if l.strip() != '']
    if r['stderr'].strip():
        errors.append(r)
        continue
    # actual output: first line is header, rest values
    hdr = act_lines[0] if act_lines else ''
    vals = act_lines[1:]
    # skip comparisons containing ellipsis
    if any('⋯' in e for e in exp):
        continue
    if len(exp) >= 2 and exp[0].split() and hdr.strip().startswith(exp[0].strip().split()[0] if exp[0].strip() else '\0'):
        # full compare including header
        if [e for e in exp] != act_lines:
            mismatch.append((r, exp, act_lines, 'full'))
    else:
        # compare last len(exp) value lines, stripped
        got = [v.strip() for v in vals[-len(exp):]] if exp else []
        if exp == [] and (vals == [] or all(v.strip()=='' for v in vals)):
            continue
        if got != [e.strip() for e in exp]:
            mismatch.append((r, exp, vals, 'vals'))
print("ERRORS:", len(errors))
for r in errors[:20]:
    print(r['cmd'])
    print(' stderr:', r['stderr'][:200].replace('\n',' | '))
print()
print("MISMATCHES:", len(mismatch))
for r, exp, got, mode in mismatch:
    print('CMD:', r['cmd'])
    print(' EXP:', exp)
    print(' GOT:', got)
    print(' mode:', mode)
    print()
EOF

import json
lines = open('/tmp/t/lnav_help.txt').read().split('\n')[2172:]

def balanced(s):
    # crude: even number of single quotes and balanced parens
    q = 0; p = 0; i = 0
    while i < len(s):
        c = s[i]
        if c == "'":
            q += 1
        elif q % 2 == 0:
            if c == '(': p += 1
            elif c == ')': p -= 1
        i += 1
    return q % 2 == 0 and p <= 0

ex = []
i = 0
while i < len(lines):
    l = lines[i]
    if l.startswith('   ;'):
        cmd = l.rstrip()
        i += 1
        while i < len(lines) and lines[i].startswith('      ') and not balanced(cmd):
            cmd += ' ' + lines[i].strip()
            i += 1
        out = []
        while i < len(lines) and lines[i].strip() != '':
            out.append(lines[i])
            i += 1
        out = [o[3:] if o.startswith('   ') else o for o in out]
        ex.append((cmd.strip(), [o.rstrip() for o in out]))
    else:
        i += 1
print(len(ex))
json.dump(ex, open('help_examples.json','w'))
EOF

args.command:
cat > /tmp/t/cmds/NOTES.md <<'NOTES_EOF'
# lnav 0.14.0 headless colon-command behavioral spec

Binary: `/workspace/executable` (`lnav 0.14.0-07efb63`).
All tests run as: `/workspace/executable -n -N [-q] -c '<cmd>' ... [file]` from `/tmp/t/cmds`.
Test files: `test.log` (8 timestamped lines, levels INFO/DEBUG/WARN/ERROR, 2024-01-15T10:00:01–08)
and `plain.txt` (5 plain text lines). `cat -A` notation: `$` = end-of-line, `M-b...` = UTF-8 bytes.

## 0. Global headless behavior (critical context)

- When stdout is NOT a TTY and no `-q` is given, lnav dumps the **top view** to stdout at
  exit: all visible (post-filter) lines from the current top-of-view line to the end.
  - After a `;SELECT`, the top view is the DB result, dumped as plain aligned columns
    (see §5 write-screen-to format), NOT the boxed table.
  - After `:sh`, top view = captured command output.
  - The dump is **suppressed** if any `-c` command already wrote to stdout
    (`:echo`, `:write-*-to -`, `:sh`, ...). Verified: `-c ':goto 3' -c ':echo hi' test.log`
    prints only `hi`.
- `-q` suppresses this exit dump entirely. `-q` does NOT suppress `:echo` output.
- Errors during `-c` execution go to **stderr**; exit code stays **0**. Subsequent `-c`
  commands still run after an error.
- Exit code **1** observed only when a file given as a CLI argument cannot be opened:
  stderr:
  ```
    error: unable to open file: /nonexistent/file.log
   reason: No such file or directory
  ```
  (`:open /nonexistent2.log` from `-c` gives `error: cannot open file: ...` + reason, exit 0.)
- Multiple `-c` options execute in order; each `:echo` output appears in order.
- `-c` args starting with `;` run SQL; starting with `:` run commands. SQL errors:
  ```
    error: failed to compile SQL statement
   reason: no such table: nosuch_table
   --> command-option:1
   | SELECT * FROM nosuch_table              
  ```
  (also `reason: near "here": syntax error` for bad syntax). Exit still 0.

## 1. Error message formats (all on stderr, exit 0)

### Unknown command (single line, no source box):
```
  error: unknown command: ‘nosuchcmd’
```
Quotes are U+2018/U+2019 (`‘’`, bytes e2 80 98 / e2 80 99). If similar commands exist,
appended (e.g. for `:head`):
```
 = note: did you mean one of the following:
           clear-all-sticky-headers - Clear all sticky header bookmarks in the current view
           hide-unmarked-lines - Hide lines that have not been bookmarked
           show-lines-before-and-after - Show lines that were hidden by the 'hide-lines' commands
           toggle-sticky-header - Toggle the sticky header state for the focused line in the current view
```
(`:echoln`, `:pwd`, `:tail` → plain unknown-command error with no note.)

### Command argument errors (multi-line box), e.g. `:filter-in` with no arg:
```
  error: expecting a regular expression to filter
 --> command-option:1
 | :filter-in                              
 = help: :filter-in pattern
         ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
           Only show lines that match the given regular expression in the
           current view
```
- `command-option:N` = 1-based index of the failing `-c` option on the command line.
- ` | ` + the original command text, right-padded with spaces to (at least) 43 columns.
- ` = help: ` + command signature line, then 8 spaces + 71 `═` (U+2550) chars,
  then 10-space-indented short description of the command (wrapped at ~70 cols).
- No trailing blank line; message ends with newline.

### Bad regex, e.g. `:filter-in [` or `:highlight [`:
```
  error: ‘[’ is not a valid regular expression
 reason: missing terminating ] for character class
 --> pattern
 | [                                           
 |  ^ missing terminating ] for character class
 = help: :filter-in pattern
         ═══...═══
           <command description>
```
- ` | ` + pattern and ` |  ^ <pcre error>` lines both right-padded to the width of the
  longest line in that block (here 47 columns total).
- `:delete-filter nosuchfilter` → single line: `  error: unknown filter -- nosuchfilter`
- `:disable-filter ERROR` (no such filter) → `  error: no such filter -- ERROR`

### Other captured single-line/simple errors:
- `:eval` (no arg): box with `  error: expecting a command or query to evaluate`
- `:unix-time` (no arg): box with `  error: expecting a unix time value`
- `:comment` (no arg): box with `  error: expecting some comment text`
- `:tag` (no arg): `  error: expecting one or more tags` (single line)
- `:annotate` (no annotations): box with `  error: no annotations available for this log message`
- `:cd /nonexistent-dir`: box with `  error: cannot access -- /nonexistent-dir` +
  ` reason: No such file or directory`
- `:redirect-to /nonexistent-dir/x.txt`: box with `  error: unable to open file -- /nonexistent-dir/x.txt`
- `:write-to` / `:write-raw-to` with no marked lines: box with
  `  error: no lines marked to write, use 'm' to mark lines`
- `:write-jsonlines-to` in TEXT view: box with
  `  error: write-jsonlines-to is only supported for the LOG and DB views`
- `:goto abc`: box with `  error: invalid argument: abc` +
  ` reason: expecting line number/percentage, timestamp, or relative time`
- `:convert-time-to UTC`: single line (this env lacks zoneinfo):
  `  error: Unable to get timezone: UTC -- discover_tz_dir failed to find zoneinfo`

## 2. :echo [-n] msg

Output goes to **stdout** (or to the `:redirect-to` file). Exit 0.

- The message is everything after `:echo ` (exactly one separating space consumed);
  the rest is VERBATIM: leading/trailing/multiple spaces preserved
  (`:echo a  b   c` → `a  b   c`; `:echo    spaced out   ` → `   spaced out   `).
- Quotes are NOT stripped: `:echo "double" 'single' mixed` → `"double" 'single' mixed`.
- `:echo` with no message → prints just `\n`.
- `-n` flag suppresses the trailing newline (`:echo -n no newline here` → no `\n`).
  Consecutive `-n` echos concatenate: `-n a` + `-n b` + `c` → `abc\n`.
- Environment variable substitution IS performed: `$HOME` and `${HOME}` expand;
  undefined vars expand to empty (`undefined $NOSUCHVAR end` → `undefined  end`;
  `$1 $2` → ` `). `$(HOME)` → `(HOME)` (a `$` before a non-var char is dropped).
- Backslash escapes the next char (prevents substitution): `\$HOME` → `$HOME`.
  `\t`, `\n` are NOT escape sequences: `tab\there` → `tabthere`, `newline\nhere` →
  `newlinenhere`; literal `\\` → `\`.
- `%s %d` pass through unformatted. `;` in message is fine (`; semicolon test` printed).
- `:eval :echo hello from eval` works — echo output via eval also goes to stdout.

## 3. :eval command

"Evaluate the given command/query after doing environment variable substitution".
- `:eval ;SELECT 1+1` → runs the SQL, result visible (table `   1+1     \n         2 \n`
  on stdout as the exit dump).
- `:eval :echo hello from eval` → `hello from eval`.
- `:eval 1+1` / `:eval 'str'` → treated as lnav command →
  `error: unknown command: ‘1+1’` WITH the full `= help: :eval command` box.
- `:eval` alone → `error: expecting a command or query to evaluate` + help box.
- Env vars substituted before execution: `:eval :echo HOME is $HOME` →
  `HOME is /opt/uiuc-agent/home`.

## 4. :filter-in / :filter-out (and related)

- Affect which lines appear in the exit dump / `:write-*` view output.
- `:filter-in ERROR` → only the 2 ERROR lines dumped. `:filter-out ERROR` → other 6.
- Multiple filters combine (AND): filter-in ERROR + filter-out timeout → 1 line.
- Adding the same filter twice: silently idempotent, no error.
- With no file loaded: no output, no error, exit 0.
- Non-matching filter → empty dump (no output at all).
- `:delete-filter <unknown>` → `error: unknown filter -- <pattern>`;
  `:disable-filter <unknown>` → `error: no such filter -- <pattern>`.
- `:filter-expr :log_level = 'error'` works (SQL expr with `:col` refs), same 2 lines.
- `:hide-lines-before 2024-01-15T10:00:04` → dump starts at that timestamp (inclusive).
- `:hide-lines-after 2024-01-15T10:00:04` → dump ends at that timestamp (inclusive).
- `:set-min-log-level error` → only ERROR lines. Invalid level (`bogus`) silently
  ignored — no error, all lines shown.
- `:goto 0` + `:mark` + `:hide-unmarked-lines` → only marked line dumped.

## 5. :write-* family

Common: `path` of `-` writes to stdout (and suppresses the exit dump). Writing to a
real file produces **no confirmation message** (no "wrote N rows") on stdout/stderr in
headless mode. Existing files are silently overwritten (`:write-to`). No `-q` effect on
the file contents. `--anonymize` replaces words with dictionary words
(sample: `2024-... INFO abaft up abashed aberrant`, leading space added, level words
anonymized for DEBUG/ERROR but timestamps/numbers/`user bob`/`id=42` partly preserved).

- `:write-to PATH` — marked lines only, raw content. No marks → error box
  `no lines marked to write, use 'm' to mark lines`. Use `:mark-expr 1` to mark all.
- `:write-raw-to [--view log|db] PATH` — same "no lines marked" requirement in log view;
  in DB view writes raw cell contents (`SELECT 1` → file/stdout content `1\n`).
- `:write-jsonlines-to [--all] PATH` — `--all` = all visible lines (no marks needed).
  One compact JSON object per line, e.g.:
  `{"log_path":"/tmp/t/cmds/test.log","log_time":"2024-01-15T10:00:01.000000","log_level":"info","log_line_link":"#msg00060ef913bc0a40-v1:3284a5bdc002d898c8b94510a62ff26c","log_time":"2024-01-15T10:00:01.000","log_level":"INFO"}`
  (note: format fields appear twice — normalized + original from the log format).
  For SQL results: `{"one":1,"two":2.5,"three":"three"}`.
  TEXT view → error `only supported for the LOG and DB views`.

## Global headless behavior (the big discoveries)

- **Exit dump**: with stdout piped and no `-q`, lnav prints the top view (filtered, from current top line to EOF) to stdout at exit. ## Command highlights

- **`:echo`**: message after the first separating space is verbatim (spaces, quotes, `;` preserved; quotes NOT stripped). `$VAR`/`${VAR}` env-substituted (undefined → empty), `\$` escapes; `\t`/`\n` are *not* escapes (`\t` → `t`). `-n` omits newline. Output → stdout.
- **`:eval`**: runs a command/query after env substitution — `:eval ;SELECT 1+1` and `:eval :echo ...` work; `:eval 1+1` → `unknown command: ‘1+1’` with full help box.
- **`:filter-in`/`:filter-out`**: change the dump/`write-*` contents; filters AND together; duplicates silently idempotent; no file → silent success.
- **`write-*`**: `-` = stdout. File writes are **silent** (no "wrote N rows") and silently overwrite. `:write-to`/`:write-raw-to` require marked lines (`error: no lines marked to write, use 'm' to mark lines`; use `:mark-expr 1`). `:write-jsonlines-to --all` needs no marks. Formats captured exactly: CSV (header row), pretty JSON (4-space indent), JSON Lines (compact), json-cols (odd leading-comma style), table (Unicode box + ANSI bold even to files/pipes), screen (plain 10-wide columns, trailing space).
- **`:goto`** takes 0-based line / `N%` / timestamp; moves dump start. **`:head`, `:tail`, `:pwd`, `:echoln` don't exist** → `error: unknown command: ‘head’` (head gets a "did you mean" note).
- **`:comment`/`:tag`**: render in the exit dump as `└ Line 0 metadata` + ` ┴ <text>` lines (markdown stripped), but not in `:write-view-to`. No-arg errors: `expecting some comment text` / `expecting one or more tags`. `:annotate` → `no annotations available for this log message`.

- **`:sh`**: runs via `/bin/bash -c`; child stdout *and* stderr both captured to lnav stdout; child exit code ignored (lnav stays 0). `:cd` affects it; bad `:cd` → `cannot access -- <dir>` box. **`:redirect-to`** captures `:echo` output to a file but not the exit dump.

lnav 0.14.0

A fancy log file viewer for the terminal.

Overview

The Logfile Navigator, lnav, is an enhanced log file viewer that takes
advantage of any semantic information that can be gleaned from the
files being viewed, such as timestamps and log levels. Using this
extra semantic information, lnav can do things like interleaving
messages from different files, generate histograms of messages over
time, and providing hotkeys for navigating through the file. It is
hoped that these features will allow the user to quickly and
efficiently zero in on problems.

regexp_capture(string, pattern)
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  A table-valued function that executes a regular-expression over a
  string and returns the captured values.  If the regex only matches a
  subset of the input string, it will be rerun on the remaining parts
  of the string until no more matches are found.
Parameters
  string    The string to match against the given pattern.
  pattern   The regular expression to match.
Results
  match_index     The match iteration.  This value
                  will increase each time a new match is found in the
                  input string.
  capture_index   The index of the capture in the
                  regex.
  capture_name    The name of the capture in the
                  regex.
  capture_count   The total number of captures in
                  the regex.
  range_start     The start of the capture in the
                  input string.
  range_stop      The stop of the capture in the
                  input string.
  content         The captured value from the
                  string.

# lnav 0.14.0 CLI behavioral notes

Binary: `/workspace/executable`, version string `lnav 0.14.0-07efb63`.
All observations made in a container as root (uid 0), no /var/log/syslog, no /usr/share/zoneinfo, no network.
Unless noted otherwise, runs used a clean default HOME (`/opt/uiuc-agent/home`).

## 1. Help / version / option parsing

- `-h` and `--help`: identical full text, written to **stderr**, stdout empty, **exit 0**.
  Saved at `/tmp/t/cli/help.txt` (2518 bytes). Extra args after `-h` are ignored
  (`-h foo bar` → exit 0, same text). `-h` beats invalid options in ANY position
  (`-h -Z` and `-Z -h` both exit 0 and print help).
- `-V` and `--version`: identical → stdout `lnav 0.14.0-07efb63\n`, exit 0.
  Extra args ignored (`-V foo bar` → exit 0).
- Invalid option `-Z` or `--bogus` → **exit 109**, stderr exactly:
  ```
    error: invalid command-line arguments
   reason: The following argument was not expected: -Z
  ```
  (no trailing help text; each line starts with exactly the shown spaces:
  two spaces before `error:`, one before `reason:`)
- Option missing its argument → **exit 114**, stderr:
  - `-c`  → `  error: invalid command-line arguments\n reason: -c: 1 required  missing\n`
    (note TWO spaces between `required` and `missing` — the arg-type name is empty)
  - `-I`  → ` reason: -I: 1 required TEXT:DIR missing`
  - `-d`  → ` reason: -d: 1 required FILE missing`
- Short flags combine: `-nN` works.
- `--` ends option parsing; following tokens are file names.

## 2. Paths embedded in `-h` output

- First line `usage: <ARGV0> [options] [logfile1 logfile2 ...]` — uses argv[0]
  **verbatim** (`./executable -h` → `usage: ./executable ...`,
  `exec -a fakeargv0` → `usage: fakeargv0 ...`, symlink `bin/mylnav` → `usage: ./bin/mylnav ...`).
- `🧭 This binary:` line — uses the **resolved real path of the executable**
  (realpath of /proc/self/exe): always `/workspace/executable`, even when invoked
  via symlink or relative path.
- Format files read from: fixed `/etc/lnav` and `/usr/etc/lnav`.
- `Configuration, session, and format files are stored in:` → `$HOME/.lnav`
  **if $HOME is set AND is an existing directory** (e.g. HOME=/tmp/fakehome → `/tmp/fakehome/.lnav`,
  HOME=/ → `/.lnav`). If $HOME is unset OR the directory does not exist → falls back to the
  **current working directory with no `.lnav` suffix** (e.g. cwd /tmp → `/tmp`).
  `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is ignored.
- Work dir line: `$TMPDIR/lnav-user-<uid>-work` (default TMPDIR=/tmp → `/tmp/lnav-user-0-work`;
  uid numeric). If TMPDIR points to a non-existent directory the process **aborts**:
  stderr `terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::filesystem::__cxx11::filesystem_error'`
  + `  what():  filesystem error: temp_directory_path: No such file or directory`, killed by
  SIGABRT → **exit 134**.
- TZ and LANG/LC_ALL have **no effect** on `-h` (emoji always emitted as UTF-8 even under LC_ALL=C).
- The Examples block lines have trailing whitespace, e.g. `     $ lnav                                  $`
  (padded with spaces to align — byte-exact via cat -A in help.txt).
- Non-ASCII characters in `-h` (task 12): exactly five distinct:
  - U+2022 `•` BULLET (7×), U+1F9ED 🧭 COMPASS (1×), U+1F4C2 📂 OPEN FILE FOLDER (4×),
    U+1F4AC 💬 SPEECH BALLOON (1×), U+1F4EB 📫 CLOSED MAILBOX WITH RAISED FLAG (1×).
  (Elsewhere the UI also uses curly quotes “ ” U+201C/U+201D in error messages.)
- Last line of help: `Version: lnav 0.14.0-07efb63`.

## 3. `-d file` debug log

`/workspace/executable -n -N -d dbg.log somefile.log` → exit 0; headless stdout still prints
the file content. Debug file for a 2-line input was ~350 KB. Line format:

```
2026-08-08T20:37:15.171215+00:00 E t0 lnav.cc:2821 unable to set locale to ''
2026-08-08T20:37:15.171310+00:00 E t0 lnav.cc:2880 failed to setup tz: discover_tz_dir failed to find zoneinfo
<blank line>
2026-08-08T20:37:15.171451+00:00 I t0 lnav.cc:2901 opening main sqlite3 (3.37.2) DB
...
2026-08-08T20:37:15.172962+00:00 I t0 lnav.cc:3290 lnav started 1
2026-08-08T20:37:15.172974+00:00 I t0 lnav.cc:3292   arg[0] = /workspace/executable
... (one line per argv entry) ...
2026-08-08T20:37:15.173072+00:00 D t0 [4828::load_config-0] lnav_config.cc:2208 skipping writing sample: root-config.json (mtimes 1786220543 >= 1776616406)
...
```

Format: `<RFC3339 ts with µs and +00:00> <LEVEL letter E/I/D> t<thread> [pid::scope-N] <file>:<line> <msg>`.
First two errors are environment-specific (empty locale, missing zoneinfo).
`-d` pointing into a non-existent directory is **silently ignored** (exit 0, normal behavior).

## 4. `-W`, `-C`, `-i`

- `-W` without `-n` tries to start the TUI → since stdout is not a TTY: **exit 1**, stderr:

   = help: pass the -n option to run lnav in headless mode or don't redirect stdout
  ```
- `-n -N -W` with clean config → exit 0, no output. With a format file missing `$schema`:
  warnings on stderr, exit 0:

- `-C` (undocumented in -h): checks config and exits. Clean → exit 0, no output.
  With the invalid badfmt installed → same two error blocks on stderr, **exit 1**.
  `-C` prints errors only, NOT warnings.
- Invalid formats under `$HOME/.lnav/formats/installed/` break EVERY subsequent run

- `-i <file.json>` with valid format json `{"fake_log":{...}}`:

  exit 0. Running again → stdout `  info: file is already installed at -- ...`, exit 0.
  A JSON that lacks required format fields (`{"badfmt":{"title":"Bad"}}`) still installs
  ("  installed -- ...", exit 0) but then poisons later runs.
- `-i` with malformed JSON → **exit 1**, stderr:

    error: unable to open configuration file: /tmp/t/cli/bad.json

  offline it prints git's fatal error + `Unable to open remote-config.json: No such file or directory`
  to stderr but still exits **0**.

## 5. `-m` management mode (all output observed with HOME=/tmp/fakehome)

- `-m` alone → **exit 1**, stderr: `  error: expecting an operation to perform` +

   = help: the available operations are:
            • apps: manage lnav apps
            • config: perform operations on the lnav configuration

            • piper: perform operations on piper storage

  (bullet `•` U+2022; note: if an invalid installed format exists, its error blocks print FIRST)
- Sub-operation names are singular: `format`, not `formats`. `-m formats list` → exit 109:
  ` reason: The following arguments were not expected: list formats`

- `-m format` → exit 1: `  error: expecting a format name to operate on` +

## 6. No-args / default-file behavior

- Container has NO `/var/log/syslog`.
- `timeout 5 lnav -n </dev/null` → **exit 1**, stderr:
  ```
    error: nothing to do
   reason: no files given or default files found
   = help: use the “-N” option to open lnav without loading any files
  ```
  (curly quotes around -N)
- `lnav -n -N </dev/null` → exit 0, no output at all.
- stdin fully closed (`0<&-`) behaves the same as `</dev/null` for both cases.
- Under a pty (`script -qec "/workspace/executable -n -N"`), exit 0 quietly.

## 7. stdin / `-t`

- `echo test | lnav -n` → stdout `test\n`, exit 0 (stdin loaded as a file; piper capture created).
- `echo piped | lnav -n -N` → **no output, exit 0** — with `-N` and no file args, stdin is NOT loaded.
- If real file args are given, piped stdin is ignored (lnav_file shows only the files), with or without `-N`.
- `lnav -n -N < /dev/null` → exit 0, no output.
- `echo test | lnav -n -t` → stdout `2026-08-08T20:38:56.886010+0000 test`.
  Format: `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.ffffff+ZZZZ` — microseconds (6 digits), numeric offset
  **without colon** (+0000). Each piped line gets its own fresh read-time timestamp
  (µs differ per line by a few µs).
- TZ effects on `-t`: /usr/share/zoneinfo missing in container, so named zones silently
  fall back to UTC (`TZ=America/New_York` → still `+0000`). POSIX-style TZ works:
  `TZ=UTC-5` → `2026-08-09T01:39:12.741078+0500 x` (offset +0500, wall clock shifted).
  (Debug log shows `failed to setup tz: discover_tz_dir failed to find zoneinfo`.)
- Piped binary data (300 random bytes) → headless prints a **hex dump** view:
  header `     File Offset  00 01 02 03 04 05 06 07  08 09 0a 0b 0c 0d 0e 0f        ASCII      `,
  then offset/hex/ASCII rows (16 bytes per row). lnav detects non-text content.
- `-` as a file arg also means stdin: lnav_file row shows filepath `stdin`, format NULL.
  (`echo hi | lnav -n -c ';SELECT filepath,format FROM lnav_file' -`)

## 8. Exit codes & exact error formats

| case | exit | stream |
|---|---|---|
| success / headless run | 0 | stdout |
| `-h`, `-V` | 0 | stderr / stdout |
| unknown option | 109 | stderr |
| option missing argument | 114 | stderr |
| `-c` value without `:`/`;`/`|` prefix | **105** | stderr |
| file not found / nothing to do / `-i` errors / TTY-required | 1 | stderr |
| `-c` runtime errors (unknown command, bad SQL, `-f` missing, `:sh` blocked) | **0** | stderr |
| bad TMPDIR | 134 (SIGABRT) | stderr |

Byte-exact samples (cat -A, `$` = EOL; note trailing-space padding to column ~40 in
` | ` snippet lines — snippet content is padded to 40 chars):

- File not found:
  ```
    error: unable to open file: /tmp/t/cli/no-such-file.log$
   reason: No such file or directory$
  ```
- `-c ':nosuchcmd'` (exit 0):
  `  error: unknown command: “nosuchcmd”$` (curly quotes U+201C/U+201D)
- `-c ';SELECT * FROM nosuchtable'` (exit 0):
  ```
    error: failed to compile SQL statement$
   reason: no such table: nosuchtable$
   --> command-option:1$
   | SELECT * FROM nosuchtable               $
  ```
- `-c ';bogus sql'` (exit 0): same shape, ` reason: near "bogus": syntax error`.
- `-c 'SELECT 1'` (no prefix, **exit 105**):
  ```
    error: invalid value for “-c” option$
   --> command-line argument$
   |  -c SELECT 1                            $
   |     ^ command type prefix is missing    $
   = help: command arguments must start with one of the following symbols to denote the type of command:$
            : - an lnav command   (e.g. :goto 42)$
            ; - an SQL statement  (e.g. ;SELECT * FROM syslog_log)$
            | - an lnav script    (e.g. |rename-stdin foo)$
  ```
- Unmatched glob arg (`'/tmp/t/cli/nomatch*.log'`, exit 1):
  ```
    error: unable to open file: /tmp/t/cli/nomatch*.log
   reason: failed to find path of “/tmp/t/cli/nomatch*.log”
   |        reason: No such file or directory
  ```
  (nested reason continuation line ` |        reason: ...`)
- Error anatomy: `  error: <msg>` / ` reason: <msg>` / ` --> <file>:<line>` /
  ` | <source snippet>` / ` = help: ...` / ` = note: ...` / ` =   note:` (extra indent
  in -W output). Some helps include a box-drawing rule of U+2500 `─` repeated
  under the command synopsis (see `:filter-in` / `:sh` help dumps).

## 9. Argument edge cases

- Same file twice → deduplicated, single lnav_file row.
- `relfile.log`, `./relfile.log`, `/tmp/t/cli/relfile.log` → all collapse to one row;
  `lnav_file.filepath` always stores the **absolute** path.
- Glob pattern passed as a single (shell-quoted) arg is expanded **by lnav**:
  `'/tmp/t/cli/dir1/*.log'` → `dir1/a.log`, `dir1/z.log` (alphabetical). No-match → exit 1 error above.
- Filenames with spaces work fine.
- Directory arg (no `-r`): loads all non-hidden regular files, alphabetical:
  a.log, b.txt, c.gz, z.log. `.hidden` NOT loaded. `c.gz` (real gzip) transparently
  decompressed. Subdirectories ignored without `-r`; with `-r`, `subdir/s.log` loads,
  ordered by full path after z.log.
- Plain-text files (format NULL in lnav_file) vs recognized logs (e.g. ISO8601 lines →
  `generic_log`). Headless stdout prints the TOP view:
  - only text files → only the LAST text-file argument's content is shown
    (`tA tB tC` → T3; `tC tA tB` → T2). Text view displays one file at a time.
  - mix of log + text files → the log view wins; text content not printed.
  - multiple log files → merged into ONE log view.
- Log view ordering: lines are ordered by their **adjusted** timestamp. Timestamps going
  backwards within one file are clamped forward to the previous line's time
  (file with 01,05,03,09 → log_time 01,05,**05**,09 — verified via
  `;SELECT log_line, log_time FROM generic_log`). Merge order of ts1+ts2 reflected that.
- `-R` also loads rotated siblings: `ts3.log` + `-R` → loads `ts3.log.1` too.
- `-S`/`--since` alone: shows lines with adjusted time ≥ given time (inclusive). Works
  sanely on both small and large files. Bad value (`-S not-a-time`) → exit 1:
  `  error: invalid 'since' time “not-a-time”\n reason: Unrecognized input`
  (straight single quotes around 'since', curly around value).
- `-U`/`--until` alone: shows lines with time ≤ given time (inclusive).
- **`-S` and `-U` TOGETHER are buggy**: on a 2000-line file (1 line/minute),
  `-S 12:00 -U 13:00` printed lines 0..180 — i.e. behaved like `-U` alone, `-S` ignored.
  On a 5-line file the combined output is erratic, e.g. (times 01,03,05,07,09):
  S=02,U=06 → {01,03,05}; S=02,U=08 → ∅; S=04,U=07 → ∅; S=04,U=09 → {05,07,09};
  S=05,U=05 → {01,03,05}. Do not rely on sane intersection semantics for small files.

## 10. `-c`, `-f`, `-e`

- `-c` repeatable, executed in given order, after files load. Prefixes:
  `:` lnav command, `;` SQL, `|` lnav script NAME (e.g. `|echo fromscript` →
  `  error: unknown script -- echo -- file not found` + ` --> command-option:1` snippet, exit 0).
- **Headless stdout rule (observed)**: `:echo` (and `:sh`) output is written immediately,
  in order. SQL result tables are only printed when NO `:echo`-style output command ran
  anywhere in the -c/-f sequence; and only the LAST SQL statement's result is shown:
  - `-c ';SELECT 1' -c ';SELECT 2' -c ';SELECT 3'` → prints only table for 3.
  - `-c ';SELECT 1' -c ':echo E'` or `-c ':echo E' -c ';SELECT 1'` → prints only `E`.
  - `-c ':echo a' -c ':echo b' -c ';SELECT 1' -c ';SELECT 2'` → prints `a`, `b` only.
  - view commands that produce no output (e.g. `:filter-in` on the LOG view) don't suppress;
    but `:filter-in` AFTER a SELECT errors (`  error: db view does not support filtering`,
    exit 0) and then nothing is dumped.
- SQL table output format: header row + data rows; columns padded with spaces, single
  space separator, trailing space at EOL; header roughly centered/right-aligned over the
  column; NULL prints as `<NULL>`; SQL expr used as column name verbatim (`1+1`).
  Numbers right-aligned; text left-aligned. log_time renders as `2026-08-08 10:00:01.000000`
  (space separator, µs).
- `-f file`: executes script lines (`:echo hi`, `;...`); same stdout rules. Missing file →
  `  error: unknown script -- <path> -- file not found` (exit 0). `-f -` reads the script
  from stdin (works).
- `-e 'printf "line1\nline2\n"'` → runs via shell, captures stdout+stderr, loads as a file;
  headless prints the captured content. lnav_file.filepath = `sh-0 printf "line1\nline2\n"`
  (`sh-<N> ` prefix + the command line). Child exit code ignored (`-e 'false'` → exit 0;
  `exit 3` + stderr → exit 0, both streams' content shown).

## 11. Environment variables

- `LNAVSECURE=1`: `-c ':sh echo hi'` → exit 0, stderr:
  ```
    error: sh -- unavailable in secure mode
   --> command-option:1
   | :sh echo hi
   = help: :sh --name=<name> cmdline
   ...
  ```
  `-e` is internally translated to `:sh` and blocked identically (snippet shows
  ` | :sh echo viaE`). `:echo`, SQL, `-f` scripts still work under LNAVSECURE.
- `NO_COLOR`: no effect on `-h` (byte-identical md5).
- `TERM=xterm-256color`: no ANSI colors appear in headless errors — all plain text.
- `HOME`: see §2 (config dir = $HOME/.lnav only if the dir exists, else cwd).
- `TMPDIR`: base for `lnav-user-<uid>-work`; nonexistent TMPDIR → abort, exit 134.
- `TZ`: affects -t timestamps only via POSIX rules (no zoneinfo in container); named zones → UTC.
- `LANG`/`LC_ALL`: no effect on -h emoji; debug log notes `unable to set locale to ''`.

## Misc

- `-H` (internal help): without `-n` → TTY error (exit 1). With `-n` dumps the full
  ~260 KB user guide to stdout, exit 0 (starts `\nlnav 0.14.0\n\nA fancy log file viewer...`).
- `-q`: does not suppress `:echo` output or error messages (observed no visible difference
  in headless).
- `-u`: stdout `No formats from git repositories found, use 'lnav -i extra' to install third-party formats`, exit 0.
- piper: piped stdin is stored under `/tmp/lnav-user-0-work/piper`, listed by `-m piper list`
  with URLs `piper://p-<md5-like hex>-000` titled “stdin”.
- `-W`/`-H` and any non-`-n` invocation with redirected stdout fail with the
  "unable to display interactive text UI / stdout is not a TTY" error, exit 1.
NOTES_EOF

# lnav 0.14.0 CLI behavioral notes

Binary: `/workspace/executable`, version string `lnav 0.14.0-07efb63`.
All observations made in a container as root (uid 0), no /var/log/syslog, no /usr/share/zoneinfo, no network.
Unless noted otherwise, runs used a clean default HOME (`/opt/uiuc-agent/home`).

## 1. Help / version / option parsing

- `-h` and `--help`: identical full text, written to **stderr**, stdout empty, **exit 0**.
  Saved at `/tmp/t/cli/help.txt` (2518 bytes). Extra args after `-h` are ignored
  (`-h foo bar` → exit 0, same text). `-h` beats invalid options in ANY position
  (`-h -Z` and `-Z -h` both exit 0 and print help).
- `-V` and `--version`: identical → stdout `lnav 0.14.0-07efb63\n`, exit 0.
  Extra args ignored (`-V foo bar` → exit 0).
- Invalid option `-Z` or `--bogus` → **exit 109**, stderr exactly:
  ```
    error: invalid command-line arguments
   reason: The following argument was not expected: -Z
  ```
  (no trailing help text; each line starts with exactly the shown spaces:
  two spaces before `error:`, one before `reason:`)
- Option missing its argument → **exit 114**, stderr:
  - `-c`  → `  error: invalid command-line arguments\n reason: -c: 1 required  missing\n`
    (note TWO spaces between `required` and `missing` — the arg-type name is empty)
  - `-I`  → ` reason: -I: 1 required TEXT:DIR missing`
  - `-d`  → ` reason: -d: 1 required FILE missing`
- Short flags combine: `-nN` works.
- `--` ends option parsing; following tokens are file names.

## 2. Paths embedded in `-h` output

- First line `usage: <ARGV0> [options] [logfile1 logfile2 ...]` — uses argv[0]
  **verbatim** (`./executable -h` → `usage: ./executable ...`,
  `exec -a fakeargv0` → `usage: fakeargv0 ...`, symlink `bin/mylnav` → `usage: ./bin/mylnav ...`).
- `🧭 This binary:` line — uses the **resolved real path of the executable**
  (realpath of /proc/self/exe): always `/workspace/executable`, even when invoked
  via symlink or relative path.
- Format files read from: fixed `/etc/lnav` and `/usr/etc/lnav`.
- `Configuration, session, and format files are stored in:` → `$HOME/.lnav`
  **if $HOME is set AND is an existing directory** (e.g. HOME=/tmp/fakehome → `/tmp/fakehome/.lnav`,
  HOME=/ → `/.lnav`). If $HOME is unset OR the directory does not exist → falls back to the
  **current working directory with no `.lnav` suffix** (e.g. cwd /tmp → `/tmp`).
  `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is ignored.
- Work dir line: `$TMPDIR/lnav-user-<uid>-work` (default TMPDIR=/tmp → `/tmp/lnav-user-0-work`;
  uid numeric). If TMPDIR points to a non-existent directory the process **aborts**:
  stderr `terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::filesystem::__cxx11::filesystem_error'`
  + `  what():  filesystem error: temp_directory_path: No such file or directory`, killed by
  SIGABRT → **exit 134**.
- TZ and LANG/LC_ALL have **no effect** on `-h` (emoji always emitted as UTF-8 even under LC_ALL=C).
- The Examples block lines have trailing whitespace, e.g. `     $ lnav                                  $`
  (padded with spaces to align — byte-exact via cat -A in help.txt).
- Non-ASCII characters in `-h` (task 12): exactly five distinct:
  - U+2022 `•` BULLET (7×), U+1F9ED 🧭 COMPASS (1×), U+1F4C2 📂 OPEN FILE FOLDER (4×),
    U+1F4AC 💬 SPEECH BALLOON (1×), U+1F4EB 📫 CLOSED MAILBOX WITH RAISED FLAG (1×).
  (Elsewhere the UI also uses curly quotes “ ” U+201C/U+201D in error messages.)
- Last line of help: `Version: lnav 0.14.0-07efb63`.

## 3. `-d file` debug log

`/workspace/executable -n -N -d dbg.log somefile.log` → exit 0; headless stdout still prints
the file content. Debug file for a 2-line input was ~350 KB. Line format:

```
2026-08-08T20:37:15.171215+00:00 E t0 lnav.cc:2821 unable to set locale to ''
2026-08-08T20:37:15.171310+00:00 E t0 lnav.cc:2880 failed to setup tz: discover_tz_dir failed to find zoneinfo
<blank line>
2026-08-08T20:37:15.171451+00:00 I t0 lnav.cc:2901 opening main sqlite3 (3.37.2) DB
...
2026-08-08T20:37:15.172962+00:00 I t0 lnav.cc:3290 lnav started 1
2026-08-08T20:37:15.172974+00:00 I t0 lnav.cc:3292   arg[0] = /workspace/executable

First two errors are environment-specific (empty locale, missing zoneinfo).
`-d` pointing into a non-existent directory is **silently ignored** (exit 0, normal behavior).

## 4. `-W`, `-C`, `-i`

- `-W` without `-n` tries to start the TUI → since stdout is not a TTY: **exit 1**, stderr:
  ```
    error: unable to display interactive text UI
   reason: stdout is not a TTY
   = help: pass the -n option to run lnav in headless mode or don't redirect stdout
  ```
- `-n -N -W` with clean config → exit 0, no output. With a format file missing `$schema`:
  warnings on stderr, exit 0:
  ```
    warning: format file is missing “$schema” property
   --> /tmp/fakehome/.lnav/formats/installed/fake_log.json
   =   note: the schema specifies the supported format version and can be used with editors to automatically validate the file
   =   help: add the following property to the top-level JSON object:
               "$schema": "https://lnav.org/schemas/format-v1.schema.json",
  ```
  With an invalid format also present (badfmt: title only) → additionally two errors
  (`“badfmt” is not a valid log format` / `no regexes specified` and
  `log message samples must be included in a format definition`, each with
  ` --> <path>:1`) and **exit 1**.
- `-C` (undocumented in -h): checks config and exits. Clean → exit 0, no output.
  With the invalid badfmt installed → same two error blocks on stderr, **exit 1**.
  `-C` prints errors only, NOT warnings.
- Invalid formats under `$HOME/.lnav/formats/installed/` break EVERY subsequent run
  (same errors on stderr, exit 1 for -m; normal `-n` runs still work but... see below).
- `-i <file.json>` with valid format json `{"fake_log":{...}}`:
  stdout `  installed -- /tmp/fakehome/.lnav/formats/installed/fake_log.json` — note the
  destination file is named after the FORMAT NAME (`fake_log`), not the input filename.
  exit 0. Running again → stdout `  info: file is already installed at -- ...`, exit 0.
  A JSON that lacks required format fields (`{"badfmt":{"title":"Bad"}}`) still installs
  ("  installed -- ...", exit 0) but then poisons later runs.
- `-i` with malformed JSON → **exit 1**, stderr:
  ```
    error: unable to open configuration file: /tmp/t/cli/bad.json
   reason: JSON parsing failed -- lexical error: invalid char in json text.
   |                                               {invalid json 
   |                            (right here) ------^
  ```
  (note trailing space after `{invalid json`; caret column points at the bad char)
- `-i` nonexistent file → exit 1:
  `  error: unable to open configuration file: ...\n reason: No such file or directory`
- `-i extra` → stdout `Cloning lnav remote config repo...`, then runs

  offline it prints git's fatal error + `Unable to open remote-config.json: No such file or directory`

## 6. No-args / default-file behavior

- Container has NO `/var/log/syslog`.
- `timeout 5 lnav -n </dev/null` → **exit 1**, stderr:
  ```
    error: nothing to do
   reason: no files given or default files found
   = help: use the “-N” option to open lnav without loading any files
  ```
  (curly quotes around -N)
- `lnav -n -N </dev/null` → exit 0, no output at all.
- stdin fully closed (`0<&-`) behaves the same as `</dev/null` for both cases.
- Under a pty (`script -qec "/workspace/executable -n -N"`), exit 0 quietly.

## 7. stdin / `-t`

- `echo test | lnav -n` → stdout `test\n`, exit 0 (stdin loaded as a file; piper capture created).
- `echo piped | lnav -n -N` → **no output, exit 0** — with `-N` and no file args, stdin is NOT loaded.
- If real file args are given, piped stdin is ignored (lnav_file shows only the files), with or without `-N`.
- `lnav -n -N < /dev/null` → exit 0, no output.
- `echo test | lnav -n -t` → stdout `2026-08-08T20:38:56.886010+0000 test`.
  Format: `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.ffffff+ZZZZ` — microseconds (6 digits), numeric offset
  **without colon** (+0000). Each piped line gets its own fresh read-time timestamp
  (µs differ per line by a few µs).
- TZ effects on `-t`: /usr/share/zoneinfo missing in container, so named zones silently
  fall back to UTC (`TZ=America/New_York` → still `+0000`). POSIX-style TZ works:
  `TZ=UTC-5` → `2026-08-09T01:39:12.741078+0500 x` (offset +0500, wall clock shifted).
  (Debug log shows `failed to setup tz: discover_tz_dir failed to find zoneinfo`.)
- Piped binary data (300 random bytes) → headless prints a **hex dump** view:
  header `     File Offset  00 01 02 03 04 05 06 07  08 09 0a 0b 0c 0d 0e 0f        ASCII      `,
  then offset/hex/ASCII rows (16 bytes per row). lnav detects non-text content.
- `-` as a file arg also means stdin: lnav_file row shows filepath `stdin`, format NULL.
  (`echo hi | lnav -n -c ';SELECT filepath,format FROM lnav_file' -`)

## 9. Argument edge cases

- Same file twice → deduplicated, single lnav_file row.
- `relfile.log`, `./relfile.log`, `/tmp/t/cli/relfile.log` → all collapse to one row;
  `lnav_file.filepath` always stores the **absolute** path.
- Glob pattern passed as a single (shell-quoted) arg is expanded **by lnav**:
  `'/tmp/t/cli/dir1/*.log'` → `dir1/a.log`, `dir1/z.log` (alphabetical). No-match → exit 1 error above.
- Filenames with spaces work fine.
- Directory arg (no `-r`): loads all non-hidden regular files, alphabetical:
  a.log, b.txt, c.gz, z.log. `.hidden` NOT loaded. `c.gz` (real gzip) transparently
  decompressed. Subdirectories ignored without `-r`; with `-r`, `subdir/s.log` loads,
  ordered by full path after z.log.
- Plain-text files (format NULL in lnav_file) vs recognized logs (e.g. ISO8601 lines →
  `generic_log`). Headless stdout prints the TOP view:
  - only text files → only the LAST text-file argument's content is shown
    (`tA tB tC` → T3; `tC tA tB` → T2). Text view displays one file at a time.
  - mix of log + text files → the log view wins; text content not printed.
  - multiple log files → merged into ONE log view.
- Log view ordering: lines are ordered by their **adjusted** timestamp. Timestamps going
  backwards within one file are clamped forward to the previous line's time
  (file with 01,05,03,09 → log_time 01,05,**05**,09 — verified via
  `;SELECT log_line, log_time FROM generic_log`). Merge order of ts1+ts2 reflected that.
- `-R` also loads rotated siblings: `ts3.log` + `-R` → loads `ts3.log.1` too.
- `-S`/`--since` alone: shows lines with adjusted time ≥ given time (inclusive). Works
  sanely on both small and large files. Bad value (`-S not-a-time`) → exit 1:
  `  error: invalid 'since' time “not-a-time”\n reason: Unrecognized input`
  (straight single quotes around 'since', curly around value).
- `-U`/`--until` alone: shows lines with time ≤ given time (inclusive).
- **`-S` and `-U` TOGETHER are buggy**: on a 2000-line file (1 line/minute),
  `-S 12:00 -U 13:00` printed lines 0..180 — i.e. behaved like `-U` alone, `-S` ignored.
  On a 5-line file the combined output is erratic, e.g. (times 01,03,05,07,09):
  S=02,U=06 → {01,03,05}; S=02,U=08 → ∅; S=04,U=07 → ∅; S=04,U=09 → {05,07,09};
  S=05,U=05 → {01,03,05}. Do not rely on sane intersection semantics for small files.

## 10. `-c`, `-f`, `-e`

- `-c` repeatable, executed in given order, after files load. Prefixes:
  `:` lnav command, `;` SQL, `|` lnav script NAME (e.g. `|echo fromscript` →
  `  error: unknown script -- echo -- file not found` + ` --> command-option:1` snippet, exit 0).
- **Headless stdout rule (observed)**: `:echo` (and `:sh`) output is written immediately,
  in order. SQL result tables are only printed when NO `:echo`-style output command ran
  anywhere in the -c/-f sequence; and only the LAST SQL statement's result is shown:
  - `-c ';SELECT 1' -c ';SELECT 2' -c ';SELECT 3'` → prints only table for 3.
  - `-c ';SELECT 1' -c ':echo E'` or `-c ':echo E' -c ';SELECT 1'` → prints only `E`.
  - `-c ':echo a' -c ':echo b' -c ';SELECT 1' -c ';SELECT 2'` → prints `a`, `b` only.
  - view commands that produce no output (e.g. `:filter-in` on the LOG view) don't suppress;
    but `:filter-in` AFTER a SELECT errors (`  error: db view does not support filtering`,
    exit 0) and then nothing is dumped.
- SQL table output format: header row + data rows; columns padded with spaces, single
  space separator, trailing space at EOL; header roughly centered/right-aligned over the
  column; NULL prints as `<NULL>`; SQL expr used as column name verbatim (`1+1`).
  Numbers right-aligned; text left-aligned. log_time renders as `2026-08-08 10:00:01.000000`
  (space separator, µs).
- `-f file`: executes script lines (`:echo hi`, `;...`); same stdout rules. Missing file →
  `  error: unknown script -- <path> -- file not found` (exit 0). `-f -` reads the script
  from stdin (works).
- `-e 'printf "line1\nline2\n"'` → runs via shell, captures stdout+stderr, loads as a file;
  headless prints the captured content. lnav_file.filepath = `sh-0 printf "line1\nline2\n"`
  (`sh-<N> ` prefix + the command line). Child exit code ignored (`-e 'false'` → exit 0;
  `exit 3` + stderr → exit 0, both streams' content shown).

## 11. Environment variables

- `LNAVSECURE=1`: `-c ':sh echo hi'` → exit 0, stderr:
  ```
    error: sh -- unavailable in secure mode
   --> command-option:1
   | :sh echo hi
   = help: :sh --name=<name> cmdline
   ...
  ```
  `-e` is internally translated to `:sh` and blocked identically (snippet shows
  ` | :sh echo viaE`). `:echo`, SQL, `-f` scripts still work under LNAVSECURE.
- `NO_COLOR`: no effect on `-h` (byte-identical md5).
- `TERM=xterm-256color`: no ANSI colors appear in headless errors — all plain text.
- `HOME`: see §2 (config dir = $HOME/.lnav only if the dir exists, else cwd).
- `TMPDIR`: base for `lnav-user-<uid>-work`; nonexistent TMPDIR → abort, exit 134.
- `TZ`: affects -t timestamps only via POSIX rules (no zoneinfo in container); named zones → UTC.
- `LANG`/`LC_ALL`: no effect on -h emoji; debug log notes `unable to set locale to ''`.

## Misc

- `-H` (internal help): without `-n` → TTY error (exit 1). With `-n` dumps the full
  ~260 KB user guide to stdout, exit 0 (starts `\nlnav 0.14.0\n\nA fancy log file viewer...`).
- `-q`: does not suppress `:echo` output or error messages (observed no visible difference
  in headless).
- `-u`: stdout `No formats from git repositories found, use 'lnav -i extra' to install third-party formats`, exit 0.
- piper: piped stdin is stored under `/tmp/lnav-user-0-work/piper`, listed by `-m piper list`
  with URLs `piper://p-<md5-like hex>-000` titled “stdin”.
- `-W`/`-H` and any non-`-n` invocation with redirected stdout fail with the
  "unable to display interactive text UI / stdout is not a TTY" error, exit 1.

Done. Findings written to `/tmp/t/cli/NOTES.md` (366 lines), with raw captures (`help.txt`, per-test `.out`/`.err` files) alongside. Summary of the key results:

**Help/version/parsing**
- `-h`/`--help` → **stderr** (not stdout!), exit 0; extra args ignored; `-h` beats invalid options in any position. `-V`/`--version` → stdout `lnav 0.14.0-07efb63`, exit 0.
- Exit codes: unknown option **109** (`The following argument was not expected: -Z`), missing option arg **114** (`-c: 1 required  missing` — note double space where the arg-type name would be), `-c` without `:`/`;`/`|` prefix **105** with a fancy `error:/reason:/ | /= help:` block, runtime `-c` errors (unknown command, bad SQL, missing `-f` file, blocked `:sh`) all exit **0**.

**Path computation in `-h`**
- `usage:` line = argv[0] verbatim; `🧭 This binary:` = realpath of /proc/self/exe (symlink-proof). Config dir = `$HOME/.lnav` only if $HOME exists as a dir, else **cwd with no suffix**; XDG ignored. Work dir = `$TMPDIR/lnav-user-<uid>-work`; nonexistent TMPDIR → SIGABRT, exit 134. TZ/LANG/NO_COLOR have no effect on `-h`; emoji always UTF-8 (•, 🧭, 📂, 💬, 📫).

**Notable behaviors**
- No `/var/log/syslog` here: `-n` alone → exit 1 "nothing to do"; `-n -N` → silent exit 0. Piped stdin is loaded only with no file args and no `-N`.
- `-t` timestamps: `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.ffffff+0000` (µs, colon-less offset), per-line fresh; named TZ silently falls back to UTC (no zoneinfo in container), POSIX TZ works.
- `-c` chains: `:echo`/`:sh` print immediately; SQL tables print only if no echo ran, and only the **last** SQL result.
- Args: dedup by absolute path; quoted globs expanded by lnav (alphabetical); dirs load non-hidden files alphabetically (gzip transparent, subdirs need `-r`); only the **last** plain-text file shows in headless, while log-format files merge into one view ordered by adjusted time (backward timestamps are clamped forward).
- **`-S` + `-U` together are buggy**: on a 2000-line file `-S` is silently ignored (behaves like `-U` alone); on tiny files results are erratic (empty or wrong windows). Each flag alone is sane and inclusive.
- `-i` installs to `$HOME/.lnav/formats/installed/<format-name>.json` (exit 0; invalid JSON exit 1 with caret-pointing error). A structurally invalid format still "installs" but then makes **every** later run (even plain `-n`) fail with exit 1. `-i extra` git-clones lnav-config, fails offline, still exit 0.
- `-m` mode documented in detail: ops `apps/config/format/piper/regex101/crash`; unknown plurals give reversed-token errors (`list formats`, exit 109); full outputs for `config get/blame`, `format get/source/test`, `piper list/clean` recorded.
- `-W` prints schema warnings (exit 0) / errors (exit 1); `-C` (undocumented) checks config, errors only. `-d` writes a ~350 KB debug log (format and first lines recorded); unwritable `-d` path silently ignored. `LNAVSECURE=1` blocks `:sh`/`-e` ("unavailable in secure mode", exit 0) but not `:echo`/SQL/`-f`.
- Piped binary data renders as a hex-dump view.
